12013.html:
Dominant risks: losses and securities-driven capital erosion. The failure model is 0.999 in all three quarters. ROA was -7.04%, -4.73% and -3.53% (T-2 to T), at the 0.5th percentile, with NIM of 1.23%. Unrealized securities losses equal 133% of Tier 1 (99.4th percentile) and long-dated assets 4.9x Tier 1. Book equity/assets went from 2.05% to -2.08% to -1.85%; mark-to-market capital from 1.17% to -3.16% to -3.55%.

Data that need checking. Negative book equity sits beside a reported leverage ratio of 11.31% and Tier 1 risk-based ratio of 35.34%; this gap should be reconciled. The credit lens reads 1.0 while the Texas ratio is only 0.88% (39.7th percentile), so the lens and its own input disagree. Loans are only 9.6% of deposits, so the 68% loan growth and the rise in CRE to 18% of capital start from a small base.

Model disagreement. The run lens is mid-range (0.52-0.53): uninsured deposits are 16%, the liquid-asset ratio is 88% and the run gap only 0.19. The failure model is reacting to losses and capital, not to deposit flight, and here it is the more relevant signal.

Questions

  1. What drives the continuing losses, and what is the plan to restore positive earnings?
  2. How does the bank reconcile negative book equity with an 11.31% leverage ratio, and can it hold its securities to maturity?
  3. Why did brokered deposits (4.8%) and swaps (4.8% of assets) appear this quarter, and what is behind the 68% loan growth?

57710.html:
Dominant risk: concentrated uninsured deposits funding long-dated securities. The run lens is 0.992, 0.988 and 0.975 (T-2 to T) and the Depositors dimension about 0.99 throughout. Uninsured deposits are 86% (98.5th percentile), average large accounts $2.77M, and the run gap 3.74 (95.1st). Unrealized securities losses equal 85% of Tier 1 (97.9th) and long-dated assets 5.2x Tier 1. Borrowings are 11.7% of assets (92.8th).

Trend. Liquidity improved: the liquid-asset ratio went 0.4%, 10.8%, 18.6% and the run gap 163.76, 6.57, 3.74. The failure model eased from 0.813 to 0.668 to 0.515. Mark-to-market capital stays thin: 2.4%, 0.04%, 2.1%. Leverage is 8.73% (16.9th).

Data gaps. Loans/deposits is 0 and CRE and construction are 0; NPLs, charge-offs, reserve coverage, loan growth and swaps are not reported. The bank appears to hold essentially no loans, so the low asset-quality score (0.071) and credit lens (0.078) reflect the absence of a loan book, not strength. The T-2 run gap of 163.76 rests on a 0.4% liquid ratio and should be verified.

Model disagreement. The failure model, trained on credit failures, has little to read here and sits mid-range; the run lens, near the top, is the more relevant signal.

Questions

  1. How concentrated are the large depositors, and how have their balances behaved under stress?
  2. How much of the securities portfolio is unencumbered and could be borrowed against without realizing losses?
  3. Can the bank confirm the T-2 liquidity figures and explain its business model with no loan book?

24735.html:
Dominant risk: uninsured deposits plus securities losses at a very large bank (99.6th size percentile). Uninsured deposits are 86% (98.5th percentile) with average large accounts of $4.18M. Unrealized securities losses equal 104% of Tier 1 (98.8th) and long-dated assets 4.8x Tier 1. Leverage is 7.96% (6.2nd percentile) and mark-to-market capital is -0.95%.

Trend: deteriorating liquidity. Run lens 0.861, 0.865, 0.922 (T-2 to T); failure model 0.439, 0.448, 0.635. Deposit growth swung from 28.9% to 3.8% to -8.4%. The liquid-asset ratio fell from 59% to 52% to 36% and the run gap rose from 1.32 to 1.42 to 2.02. Borrowings rose from 1.75% to 6.45% to 7.45% of assets. Mark-to-market capital went from +1.25% to -1.24% to -0.95%.

Credit is not the issue. NPLs+OREO are 0.19%, the Texas ratio 0.79%, reserves cover problem loans 4.6x, and ROA is 0.96%.

Model disagreement. The run lens has been high for all three quarters; the failure model, trained on credit-driven failures, stayed mid-range and only rose this quarter, coinciding with the deposit outflow and liquidity drain. It still sits well below the run lens.

Questions

  1. Which depositors are leaving, and what further outflow does the bank expect?
  2. How much remaining liquidity is unencumbered and usable same-day, and what borrowing capacity is pre-positioned?
  3. Would selling securities to meet outflows crystallize losses large enough to impair capital?

20884.html:
Dominant risks: credit, run and rate risk together, all high. Failure model 0.868, 0.931, 0.919 (T-2 to T); run lens 0.956, 0.962, 0.975; credit lens 0.879, 0.884, 0.948.

Credit. CRE is 368% of capital (79.7th percentile). The Texas ratio was 7.2% and 7.0%, then 11.3% (94.1st); NPLs+OREO rose to 1.99% (90.8th). Reserve coverage fell from 2.12x to 1.30x.

Funding and liquidity. Uninsured deposits are 62% (96.5th); the run gap rose from 2.81 to 3.46 to 4.35 (96.6th); the liquid-asset ratio fell from 19% to 17% to 13%. Deposits shrank every quarter (-9.2%, -14.8%, -7.6%).

Rate risk and capital. Mark-to-market capital went from -0.01% to -1.79% to -2.47%. Unrealized securities losses equal 73% of Tier 1 and estimated loan losses at market prices 59%; long-dated assets are 5.4x Tier 1 (87.1st). Leverage is 8.11% (7.9th). Efficiency is 79% and ROA 0.74%.

Model agreement. The two models agree: the failure model picks up the credit deterioration and the run lens the deposit outflow. The combination, CRE losses arriving while deposits leave and capital is negative at market prices, is the core concern.

Questions

  1. Which CRE loans drove the rise in problem assets, and is the reserve adequate now that coverage is 1.30x?
  2. What is driving the persistent deposit outflow, and what does the contingency funding plan assume if it continues?
  3. Has the bank stress-tested capital under combined CRE losses and forced securities sales?

13584.html:
Dominant risks: thin capital, weak credit and long-dated assets at a small bank (9.9th size percentile). Failure model 0.998, 0.996, 1.0 (T-2 to T); credit lens 0.997, 0.996, 0.995.

Capital. Book equity/assets was 1.17%, -0.82% and 0.65%, near the bottom of peers (0.7th percentile at T), against a reported leverage ratio of 8.96%. Mark-to-market capital is -5.38% (1.5th). Unrealized securities losses equal 93% of Tier 1 (98.4th) and long-dated assets 6.5x Tier 1 (94.4th).

Credit. NPLs+OREO 3.7% (95.2nd), Texas ratio 19.3% (97.9th), reserve coverage only 57% (5.5th). Net charge-offs are slightly negative (net recoveries) in every quarter despite elevated problem assets.

Earnings. ROA 0.15% and efficiency 94% (94.9th) leave little capacity to absorb losses.

Funding. Uninsured deposits are low (15%) and the run gap 0.49. Borrowings are 11.4% of assets (92.2nd). Swaps are not reported.

Model disagreement. The failure model is at its maximum; the run lens is mid-range (0.654, 0.657, 0.603) because deposits are mostly insured. The risk is solvency, not a deposit run; reliance on borrowings is the funding item to watch.

Questions

  1. How does the bank reconcile near-zero or negative book equity with an 8.96% leverage ratio, and could it be forced to realize its securities losses?
  2. Why are charge-offs negative while problem assets are 3.7% and reserves cover only 57%?
  3. What collateral backs the borrowings, and how would a valuation haircut affect liquidity?

27332.html:
Dominant risks: thin capital, large market-value losses, CRE concentration and uninsured funding, all worsening. Failure model 0.974, 0.981, 0.997 (T-2 to T); run lens 0.961, 0.974, 0.984; credit lens 0.781, 0.832, 0.915.

Capital and rate risk. Leverage is 5.27% and Tier 1 risk-based 9.45% (both 0.5th percentile). Mark-to-market capital fell from -3.9% to -7.1% to -9.3% (0.1st). Unrealized securities losses equal 133% of Tier 1 and estimated loan losses at market prices 129%; long-dated assets are 10.2x Tier 1 (99.5th).

Credit and growth. CRE is 487% of capital (93.8th) and construction 80% (82.2nd), yet loans grew 25%. The Texas ratio rose from 4.1% to 4.5% to 5.1% (81.7th).

Funding. Uninsured deposits are 64% (96.7th). The run gap rose from 2.52 to 3.09 to 3.65; the liquid-asset ratio fell from 22% to 18% to 15%; borrowings rose from 5.0% to 7.4% to 12.2% of assets. ROA slid from 0.57% to 0.49% to 0.20%.

Model agreement. Both models agree and both worsened every quarter. This is a combined credit, rate and run vulnerability with little capital buffer.

Questions

  1. Capital is deeply negative at market prices; what is the plan to raise capital or shrink the balance sheet?
  2. Why is the bank growing CRE and construction lending 25% while its capital ratios are at the bottom of peers?
  3. What borrowing capacity remains after the recent increase, and would it cover a significant uninsured outflow?

8758.html:
Dominant risk: rapidly deteriorating credit at a small bank (8.1st size percentile). NPLs+OREO rose from 4.8% to 10.5% to 12.2% (97.5th percentile); the Texas ratio from 28.7% to 65.4% to 78.5% (99.6th). Past-due loans climbed from 0.21% to 0.88% to 1.13%. Reserve coverage is only 14% (0.5th), and net charge-offs remain high at 1.5%. CRE is just 1% of capital, so the problems sit elsewhere in the loan book.

Liquidity, newly weaker. The liquid-asset ratio fell from 35% to 29% to 14% and the run gap rose from 0.93 to 1.30 to 2.08 (82nd). Loans grew 24% this quarter. Uninsured deposits are 31%.

Capital. Leverage is 8.05% (7.2nd percentile). Mark-to-market capital moved from +1.1% to -0.6% to -1.3%; unrealized securities losses equal 56% of Tier 1. ROA is still 0.86%.

Model view. The failure model (0.99, 0.999, 1.0) and credit lens (about 0.99) agree: this is a classic credit case. The run lens is also high (0.818, 0.876, 0.867) as liquidity drains, adding a second front rather than disagreeing.

Questions

  1. Which loan segments make up the 12.2% problem assets, and why do reserves cover only 14% of them?
  2. Why did the bank grow loans 24% and run down liquidity while problem assets rose from 4.8% to 12.2%?
  3. Is ROA of 0.86% credible at these problem levels; is interest on non-performing loans still being accrued?

5817.html:
Dominant risks: rate exposure and wholesale funding, with a sudden credit jump this quarter. The failure model is 0.998-0.999 in all three quarters. Long-dated assets are 7.8x Tier 1 (98.3rd percentile), unrealized securities losses 94% of Tier 1 (98.5th), and mark-to-market capital -3.3%. Brokered deposits are 28.6% (97.3rd), borrowings 8.5% of assets (85.9th), and swaps 18.7% of assets. Deposits grew 34% (95.3rd).

Credit change. The credit lens jumped from 0.076 to 0.299 to 0.972. NPLs+OREO went from 0.0% to 0.05% to 2.12% and the Texas ratio from 0.0% to 0.26% to 11.9% (94.6th). Reserve coverage fell to 56% (from 22.46x at T-1). The T-2 NPL figure of exactly zero, with reserve coverage not reported, should be checked.

Earnings are strong: ROA 1.24%, efficiency 49%.

Model disagreement. The failure model was already near the top before credit deteriorated, so it was reading capital, rate and funding structure rather than credit. The run lens is moderate (0.635, 0.666, 0.593) because uninsured deposits are only 18% and the run gap 0.47; it does not capture the risk that brokered funding fails to roll.

Questions

  1. What caused problem assets to rise from 0.05% to 2.12% in one quarter, and is the reserve adequate?
  2. How much brokered funding matures within a year, and could the bank replace it if credit losses reduce capital?
  3. What do the swaps hedge, and how much of the long-dated exposure do they offset?

10528.html:
Dominant risks: a shrinking liquidity buffer against uninsured deposits, plus construction concentration. Run lens 0.972, 0.964, 0.979 (T-2 to T). The liquid-asset ratio fell from 13% to 11% to 7.0% (4.5th percentile) and the run gap rose from 3.92 to 4.18 to 6.17 (98.7th). Uninsured deposits are 47% (89.9th) with average large accounts of $1.14M. Borrowings appeared this quarter at 3.6% of assets.

Credit. Construction loans are 74% of capital (79.7th) and CRE 164%. NPLs+OREO are 1.58% (88th), the Texas ratio 6.8% (87.1st), and reserve coverage 75% (8.2nd). Credit lens 0.978, 0.923, 0.925.

Earnings and capital. Earnings are a strength: ROA 1.89% (92.6th), efficiency 48%. Unrealized securities losses fell from 69% to 29% to 24% of Tier 1, and mark-to-market capital is near zero (-0.13%). Book equity/assets is low at 4.57% (5.5th) against 9.50% leverage.

Model view. Failure model 0.987, 0.898, 0.914. The models broadly agree; strong earnings may hold the failure model slightly below the run lens, which keys on the falling liquid buffer.

Questions

  1. Why has the liquid-asset ratio fallen to 7%, and what contingent funding is in place?
  2. How are the construction projects performing, and why do reserves cover only 75% of problem assets?
  3. Who are the larger uninsured depositors, and are any of them linked to construction or CRE borrowers?

58410.html:
Dominant risk: severe credit problems funded by brokered and borrowed money. Failure model 0.999-1.0; credit lens 0.998, 0.992, 0.997. NPLs+OREO are 31.2% (97.7th percentile), up from 14.0% at T-1. The Texas ratio is 200% (99.6th): problem assets are about double capital plus reserves. Reserve coverage is 3.6% (0.2nd). Loans shrank 46%, 31% and 10% across the three quarters.

Funding. Brokered deposits are 55.5% (98.1st), borrowings 23.7% of assets (99.1st), loans/deposits 127%. Deposits grew 45.5% and average large accounts are $6.86M.

Data concerns. Tier 1 risk-based capital is not reported in any quarter. Past-due loans spike to 10.8% at T-1 against 0.8% and 1.05% either side. A 31.2% problem-asset level alongside 15.44% leverage, 3.6% reserve coverage and positive ROA (0.90%) is hard to reconcile and should be verified before interpretation. NIM is 6.17% (99.0th).

Model disagreement. The run lens is mid-range (0.683, 0.510, 0.478) because securities losses are negligible (1.2% of Tier 1), mark-to-market capital is positive (3.8%) and uninsured deposits fell from 64% to 42%. Its inputs do not capture brokered or borrowed funding, so it likely understates funding risk here; the failure model is the better guide.

Questions

  1. Can the bank reconcile its problem-asset figures with its reserves, capital and reported earnings?
  2. Why is Tier 1 risk-based capital not reported?
  3. How much brokered and borrowed funding matures within a year, and can it be rolled once credit losses are recognized?

57053.html:
Dominant risk: uninsured deposit concentration, now with outflows. Very large bank (99.3rd size percentile). Uninsured deposits are 90% (98.6th percentile), average large accounts $3.07M, and the run gap 2.56, 2.75, 3.08 (T-2 to T; 92.1st). Run lens steady at 0.857, 0.843, 0.847; Depositors dimension 0.994.

Trend. Deposit growth swung from 21.7% to 7.6% to -16.5% (1.8th percentile). Borrowings jumped from 1.5% to 1.4% to 10.4% of assets, brokered deposits rose to 4.3%, and loans/deposits rose from 70% to 72% to 85%. The failure model moved from 0.135 to 0.109 to 0.326.

Other risks. CRE is 350% of capital (76.8th). Tier 1 risk-based capital of 11.20% (8.7th) and leverage of 8.79% (17.9th) are below most peers. Credit quality is sound (NPLs+OREO 0.32%, Texas ratio 2.3%), mark-to-market capital is positive (2.3%), efficiency strong (32%), and long-dated assets modest (1.2x Tier 1).

Model disagreement. Large. The failure model, trained mostly on credit failures, sees clean loans and good earnings and stays low; the run lens flags the uninsured base. The deposit outflow and its replacement with borrowings are exactly what the failure model is not built to see.

Questions

  1. Which depositors left, and how concentrated is the remaining uninsured base by client or sector?
  2. What collateral backs the new borrowings, and how much capacity remains?
  3. How would CRE losses at 350% of capital interact with a further deposit outflow?

8140.html:
Dominant risks: tightening liquidity and rate-driven capital erosion. Run lens 0.935, 0.935, 0.980 (T-2 to T); failure model 0.910, 0.936, 0.949. The liquid-asset ratio fell from 25% to 18% to 16% and the run gap rose from 1.34 to 1.62 to 1.99 (80.4th percentile), even though uninsured deposits are moderate (34%). Mark-to-market capital went from +0.58% to -2.45% to -1.82%; unrealized securities losses equal 49% of Tier 1 (87.5th) and long-dated assets 4.6x Tier 1.

Credit is moderate: NPLs+OREO 0.36% and Texas ratio 1.48%, but past-due loans rose from 0.24% to 0.37% to 0.47% (78.6th). Construction is 29% of capital. Credit lens 0.457, 0.438, then 0.578.

Earnings. Efficiency is 76% (78.8th) and ROA slipped from 1.05% to 0.99% to 0.91%; loans are shrinking (-3.0%).

Data gap. Tier 1 risk-based capital is not reported in any quarter, which limits the capital assessment. Book equity/assets is 5.32% (9.1st) against 9.86% leverage.

Model view. Both models are high. The failure model reads high despite moderate credit, so it appears to be weighting capital and earnings; the run lens is driven by the shrinking liquid buffer and market-value losses.

Questions

  1. Why is Tier 1 risk-based capital not reported?
  2. What is driving the steady fall in liquid assets, and how much of what remains is pledged?
  3. Which loans account for the rise in past-due balances?

59017.html:
Dominant risks: rate exposure in the loan book and uninsured funding at a very large, fast-growing bank (99.7th size percentile). Estimated loan losses at market prices equal 130% of Tier 1 (96.5th percentile), up from 94% and 104%; long-dated assets are 7.3x Tier 1 (97.3rd). Mark-to-market capital fell from -1.36% to -3.13% to -4.75% (2.5th). Uninsured deposits are 68% (97.3rd), the run gap 4.45 (96.8th), the liquid-asset ratio 12.6%, and loans/deposits 95%.

Growth. Loans grew 23%, 24% and 24% (T-2 to T) while deposit growth slowed from 23% to 19% to 13%. Brokered deposits rose from 0.4% to 2.9% to 3.0%.

Credit is very clean: NPLs+OREO 0.07%, net charge-offs 0.0%, Texas ratio 0.59%, reserves 7.2x problem loans. CRE is 211% of capital.

Capital. Leverage 8.51% (13th) and Tier 1 risk-based 11.56% (11.5th) are below most peers.

Model disagreement. The run lens is high (0.894, 0.895, 0.905); the failure model is moderate (0.727, 0.667, 0.705), as expected for a model trained on credit failures facing a bank with almost no problem loans. The vulnerability is rate and funding: a deposit outflow could force recognition of market-value losses.

Questions

  1. What is the rate profile of the long-dated loans, and how is it hedged given swaps are zero?
  2. How will 24% loan growth be funded as deposit growth slows?
  3. How concentrated are the uninsured depositors, and how much contingent funding is pre-arranged?
